div.p: Many thanks. Will send the book after New Year. I hope Mrs Dyer sent you the music. I would ring her up again but hardly like to do so from what she told me of her husband’s condition. What do you think? If you wish I will.
To Mrs Pound, yourself and Omar Ezrasson in the name of all here

div.note: The face of this holiday card, probably misdated by JJ “23.xi.37,” shows a color pen-and-ink drawing of an elderly couple sitting comfortably by the fire with their dog and cat, and contains the printed greeting, “Joyeux Noël et Meilleurs Voeux pour la nouvelle année” (Fr. “Merry Christmas and Best Wishes for the new year”). The artist is Harry Eliott, born Charles Edmond Hermet (1882-1959), a well-known French painter and illustrator whose Victorian-style images appeared in magazines and books, including editions of Charles Dickens and Jack London.

JJ planned to send Pound a copy of the play, Michael Kramer, by the German social realist Gerhart Hauptmann (1862-1946), for Hauptmann to sign. Hauptmann often spent the winter months in Rapallo, where Pound had lived with his wife Dorothy since 1924-1925. (For additional details, see JJ to Pound 5 December 1937, notes.)

Louise Berta Mosson Hanson-Dyer, née Smith (1884-1962), was an Australian pianist and harpist, music publisher, and wealthy patron of the arts who founded the music publishing company, Éditions de l’Oiseau-Lyre (Lyrebird Press), in Paris in 1932. Pound wanted to obtain from her an edition of string sonatas by the English composer, Henry Purcell (1659-1695). (For a fuller account, see JJ to Pound 5 December 1937, notes.)

James Dyer (ca. 1860-1938), a wealthy Scottish businessman who had made a fortune in Melbourne, Australia, as an importer of linoleum, married Louise Smith (“Mrs Dyer”) in 1911. He was very ill at the time of the present letter and died on 10 January 1938. (For additional details, see JJ to Pound, 5 December 1937, notes.)

Omar Shakespear Pound (1926-2010), the son of Dorothy Pound, was born in Paris and registered at birth by Ezra and Dorothy as an American citizen. (For additional details, see JJ to Pound, 9 November 1932, notes.)

“Buon Ceppo” (It. literally “Good log”) is an Italian Christmas greeting that refers to the traditional Yule log. In the Tuscan tradition, a log (usually oak) is put into the fireplace the night before Christmas. A large one is preferred, in the hope that it will burn for the following 12 days, after which time the log is transferred to the dining table. Ideally, the fire will have burned a hole in the center of the log, which is where children then find their gifts. This tradition was not observed in Trieste in Joyce’s time, but he may have heard about it from his Triestine acquaintances. By wishing someone “Buon Ceppo” one simply expresses greetings of the season in Tuscany. (Thanks to Fulvio Rogantin and Elisa Susmel for an explanation of this phrase.)
